sections.title: Prologue
sections.html:
Prologue

Three years ago.

The mountain took my husband on a Tuesday in October.

That's what I told the search and rescue team, and the county sheriff, and the reporter from the Billings Gazette, and his mother. The mountain took him. Like the mountain was a person. Like it reached down one gray afternoon and plucked Daniel Mercer off the ridge above Kestrel Lake and simply kept him.

They searched for nine days. Helicopters, dogs, sixty volunteers in orange vests walking the slopes in lines. On the fourth day, a ranger found his hat snagged on a juniper bush two hundred feet below the cliff edge. On the sixth day, a dog found his water bottle in a creek. On the ninth day, the snow came, and they called it off.

"I'm so sorry, Mrs. Mercer," the ranger said. He was young and sunburned and he couldn't look at me. "Sometimes the mountain doesn't give them back."

I cried. I cried in the ranger station and I cried in the motel and I cried at the memorial service in Billings, where Daniel's mother sat in the front row and didn't cry at all. She just watched me. The whole service, she watched me, with her son's gray eyes.

I cried in all the right places.

I've always been good at that.

sections.title: Chapter 1
sections.html:
Chapter 1

Rule #1: The generator runs from six until midnight. When the lights go out, stay in bed.

"I don't remember entering a contest," I say.

Owen grins at me across the front seat of the rental Jeep. We've been driving for four hours since Bozeman, the last hour on gravel, the last twenty minutes on something that barely deserves to be called a road. Pines crowd both sides, so tall and dark they block the sky. My phone lost its signal fifty miles ago.

"You didn't," he says. "I entered for you. You were asleep on the couch and I was scrolling, and there it was. Win a week at Stillwater Cabin. Total solitude. Nine rules. One unforgettable stay." He wiggles his eyebrows. "I thought, my wife deserves unforgettable."

My wife. Six weeks, and it still sounds like a word from somebody else's life.

I met Owen Pryce five months ago in a coffee shop in Denver. He spilled his cold brew on my laptop, then spent forty minutes helping me dry it with napkins and a hair dryer from the bathroom. He was funny and warm and a little clumsy, with sandy hair that fell in his eyes and a crooked smile that made my stomach drop. He was an architect. He was divorced, no kids. He liked old movies and bad puns and making me pancakes at midnight.

He asked me to marry him on our third month. I said yes before he finished the question.

My friends said it was too fast. My friends didn't know what it's like to spend three years as the widow everyone whispers about.

"Nine rules," I say. "That's the part that bugs me. What kind of vacation has rules?"

"The kind in the middle of nowhere, with bears." He reaches over and squeezes my knee. "Come on, Han. No phones, no internet, no neighbors. Just you and me and a woodstove." He smiles his crooked smile. "Where's your sense of adventure?"

I look down at the orange satellite messenger clipped to my backpack strap on the floor. A little rectangle of plastic the size of a deck of cards. It can send an SOS from anywhere on earth, straight to a satellite. I bought it the week Owen told me about the trip.

"Right here," I say, and tap it.

Owen laughs. "My wife, the Girl Scout."

* * *

Stillwater Cabin sits at the end of the road, at the edge of a long, narrow meadow. Beyond the meadow, the valley drops away toward a lake the color of slate, and beyond the lake, mountains. Real mountains, jagged and gray, already capped with the first snow of the season.

I know those mountains.

The cabin is small and handsome, built of dark logs with a green metal roof and a stone chimney. A porch runs along the front, with two chairs and a stack of firewood. Behind it, there's a small shed that hums. The generator. And a little way off, half sunk into the slope, there's a squat wooden door set into a mound of earth, with a padlock.

A woman is waiting on the porch.

She's in her sixties, tall and rawboned, with a long gray braid and a face like weathered wood. She wears a canvas coat and heavy boots, and there's a rifle leaning against the porch rail beside her. She doesn't smile when we get out of the Jeep.

"Mara Voss," she says. "I own the place. You found it."

"We found it," Owen says cheerfully, holding out his hand. "Owen Pryce. And this is my wife, Hannah."

Mara takes his hand. Then she turns to me, and her gray eyes move over my face, slow and careful, the way you'd study a map.

"Hannah," she says.

"Hi." I smile. "Thank you for having us. It's beautiful."

"It is." She doesn't let go of my hand quite as fast as she let go of Owen's. "I live across the valley. The lodge with the red roof, you can see it from the porch on a clear day. If you need me, there's a radio inside. Channel nine." She finally releases me. "Everything else is in the binder. Read it tonight."

"The rules," I say.

Mara looks at me for a long moment.

"The rules," she says, "are what keep people alive out here."

sections.title: Chapter 2
sections.html:
Chapter 2

Rule #3: If you hear your spouse calling your name from the trees at night, do not go outside. Your spouse is in bed with you.

The binder is red, and fat, and full of things like how to prime the water pump and where the spare lantern mantles are kept. The rules are on the first page, typed in a plain font and slipped into a plastic sleeve.

STILLWATER CABIN: RULES OF YOUR STAY

1. The generator runs from six until midnight. When the lights go out, stay in bed.

2. Lock the door at dusk. Do not unlock it until the sun clears the ridge.

3. If you hear your spouse calling your name from the trees at night, do not go outside. Your spouse is in bed with you.

4. Do not feed anything that comes to the porch.

5. The radio is for emergencies only. Channel 9. Mara will answer.

6. Do not hike past the red blazes.

7. Keep the woodstove burning. The nights here can kill you.

8. The root cellar is not part of your stay.

9. If one of you leaves the cabin at night, the other must not follow.

Owen reads them aloud in a spooky campfire voice while I make spaghetti on the propane stove. By number three, he's laughing so hard he can barely get the words out.

"Your spouse is in bed with you," he wails, waving his arms. "Oooooh!"

"Stop it." I throw a dish towel at him. I'm laughing too. Mostly. "It's creepy."

"It's marketing. It's a gimmick! Nine rules, one unforgettable stay." He tosses the binder on the table. "I bet she's got a speaker hidden in a tree somewhere, playing spooky noises for the guests. Five-star reviews on Tripadvisor."

"Then why would she tell us not to go outside?"

"Because that's what makes it scary." He comes up behind me and wraps his arms around my waist and puts his chin on my shoulder. "Don't worry. If a scary voice calls you from the woods, I'll protect you."

"Even if it's your voice?"

"Especially if it's my voice." He kisses my neck. "Because I'll be right here."

* * *

At midnight, the generator stops.

I'm half asleep, curled against Owen's back in the big log bed, when the low hum from the shed dies, and the little lamp on the dresser clicks off, and the dark comes down.

I've never known dark like this. Not in Denver, not in Billings, not anywhere. It's a total, pressing blackness, like being sealed in a box. I hold my hand in front of my face and see nothing. The only light is the dull red glow from the woodstove in the next room, leaking under the bedroom door.

I lie there listening to Owen breathe. Slow and even. Asleep.

And outside, from the trees at the edge of the meadow, someone calls my name.

"Hannah."

My whole body goes rigid.

"Hannah. Come out. It's cold."

It's a man's voice. Faint and far away and a little muffled, like it's coming through fog.

I know that voice.

I heard it every day for six years. I heard it say I do in a courthouse in Billings. I heard it whisper my name in the dark of a hundred bedrooms. I heard it on the last morning, in the parking lot at the trailhead, saying, See you on the other side, Han.

It's Daniel.

My dead husband is calling me from the trees.

"Hannah. Please. I'm so cold."

I grab Owen's shoulder and shake him. Hard. "Owen. Owen, wake up."

He mumbles something and rolls over. His hand finds my arm in the dark. Warm. Solid. Real.

Your spouse is in bed with you.

"What's wrong?" he mumbles.

"Do you hear that?"

We both lie still. I hold my breath. I listen so hard my ears ring.

Silence. Nothing but the tick of the woodstove and the wind in the pines.

"Hear what?" Owen says.

"There was a voice. Outside. Calling my name."

He's quiet for a second. Then he laughs softly and pulls me against his chest. "Told you. Speaker in a tree. Five stars." He kisses the top of my head. "Go to sleep, Han. I'm right here."

I lie awake against him until the window turns gray. He falls back asleep in about four minutes.

I don't.

Because I've been listening to the voices of the dead for three years. And I know the difference between a sound effect and a man.

sections.title: Chapter 3
sections.html:
Chapter 3

Rule #2: Lock the door at dusk. Do not unlock it until the sun clears the ridge.

In the morning, the valley is gold and blue and so beautiful it hurts. Frost on the meadow. Mist lifting off the lake. A hawk turning slow circles over the ridge. I stand on the porch with my coffee, wrapped in a wool blanket, and I look at the mountains across the water.

The tallest one has a long, sharp ridge running along its shoulder like the spine of an animal. At the end of the ridge, where it drops away into cliffs, there's a rock formation the locals call the Anvil.

That's where Daniel disappeared.

I didn't know, when Owen showed me the contest page on his laptop. The pictures were all close-ups: the cabin, the porch, the woodstove, a steaming mug on a windowsill. Kestrel Valley, Montana. I thought, That's a coincidence. Montana is a big state. There must be a dozen valleys with cabins in them.

But there's only one Anvil.

"Beautiful, huh?" Owen comes out onto the porch with his own coffee and stands beside me. "What are you looking at?"

"Nothing. Just the mountains."

I haven't told Owen about Daniel. Not really. He knows I was married before. He knows my husband died. He thinks it was an accident, back in Colorado, and I've never corrected him. When he asks, I change the subject, and he's kind enough to let me.

I didn't want him to Google me. I didn't want him to find the articles. Widow Collects $1.2 Million Insurance Payout After Husband Vanishes on Montana Peak. I didn't want him to read the comments, which were worse.

I didn't want him to look at me the way Daniel's mother did.

"Han." Owen puts his hand on my back. "You're shaking."

"It's cold."

"Come inside. I'll make pancakes."

He goes in. I stay on the porch a little longer, looking at the Anvil. And then I look down at the porch boards by my feet.

There's something on the top step. Small and silver, glinting in the morning sun.

I set down my coffee. I crouch and pick it up.

It's a carabiner. The oval kind climbers use, scuffed and old. There's a strip of red electrical tape wrapped around the spine, the way some climbers mark their gear so they don't mix it up with someone else's.

Daniel marked all his gear with red tape.

I close my hand around it so tightly the metal bites into my palm. The door was locked all night. I checked it twice. Rule two.

Whoever left this didn't need to come inside.

They just needed me to find it.

sections.title: Chapter 4
sections.html:
Chapter 4

Rule #4: Do not feed anything that comes to the porch.

Mara comes by in the afternoon, in an old Ford truck with a plow blade on the front, to drop off firewood and check the generator. Owen helps her unload the wood. I watch them from the window. They talk easily, laughing about something. At one point Mara puts her hand on his arm.

When Owen goes around back to stack the logs, I go out on the porch.

"Sleep well?" Mara asks.

"Not really." I lean on the rail. "I heard something. Last night. In the trees."

She doesn't look surprised. She takes a pair of work gloves out of her back pocket and pulls them on, one finger at a time. "Rule three."

"Somebody was calling my name."

"The wind does strange things in this valley. Comes down off the peaks and whistles through the pines. People hear all kinds of things." She looks up at me. "What did you hear, Hannah?"

"A man's voice."

"Whose?"

I don't answer.

Mara nods slowly, as if I did. "Grief does strange things too," she says. "Owen told me you lost your first husband."

My stomach drops. "He told you that?"

"On the phone, when he booked. He said you'd had a hard few years." She pulls the second glove tight. "I'm sorry for your loss."

"Thank you."

"Was it sudden?"

"Yes."

"Those are the worst. The sudden ones. You never get to say goodbye." Mara's gray eyes are steady on mine. "I lost a son, you know. Three years ago."

The wind moves through the pines. Somewhere behind the cabin, Owen is whistling, stacking logs.

"I'm sorry," I say. My voice sounds strange, even to me.

"Everyone's sorry." Mara picks up an armful of kindling and carries it to the woodbox by the door. "Keep that stove going tonight, Hannah. It's supposed to drop to ten degrees." At the steps, she pauses. "And if anything comes to the porch, don't feed it. No matter how hungry it looks."

* * *

That evening, at dusk, a fox comes to the porch.

It's thin and ragged, with a scabby tail and one torn ear. It sits at the bottom of the steps and looks at me through the window with bright black eyes. It doesn't run when I come to the glass. It just sits there, watching.

"Aw," Owen says, coming up behind me. "He's hungry."

"Rule four."

"Rule four is for bears." He's already reaching for the leftover spaghetti. "It's a fox, Han. Look at him. He's starving."

"Owen, don't."

But he's already opening the door, and tossing a handful of cold noodles out onto the porch, and the fox darts forward and gobbles them up, and then it looks up at me through the open door.

And I swear, for just a second, it looks like it's smiling.

Then it's gone into the dark, and Owen locks the door behind it, and laughs.

In the morning, the fox is on the porch again. Lying on the top step. On its side.

Its throat has been cut.

sections.title: Chapter 5
sections.html:
Chapter 5

Rule #9: If one of you leaves the cabin at night, the other must not follow.

Owen buries the fox at the edge of the meadow. He's pale and quiet all morning.

"A coyote," he says. "Or an owl. Something got it."

"Owls don't cut throats."

"Hannah." He puts down the shovel and looks at me. "What do you want me to say? That some psycho came up to our porch in the middle of the night with a knife and killed a fox? Why? Why would anybody do that?"

Because we fed it. Because we broke a rule.

I don't say it. I don't have to. I can see in his face that he's thinking it too.

* * *

That night, at 12:40, I wake up alone.

The generator's off. The room is black. I reach across the bed for Owen, and my hand finds cold sheets, and a dent in the pillow where his head was.

"Owen?"

No answer.

I sit up. My heart is thudding. The bedroom door is open a crack, and the woodstove glows red through it. I can see the dark shapes of the living room beyond. The table, the chairs, the couch.

Empty.

"Owen?"

The front door is closed. But the deadbolt, which I locked myself at dusk, which I checked twice, is turned to open.

He went outside.

If one of you leaves the cabin at night, the other must not follow.

I stand at the door in my socks, one hand on the cold iron latch. Outside, the wind is moving in the trees. I can hear it hissing through the pine needles, rising and falling.

And under it, faint, from the edge of the meadow:

"Hannah."

Daniel's voice.

"Hannah, it's so dark out here. Come find me."

I take my hand off the latch.

I back away from the door, one step, two, until my legs hit the couch and I sit down hard. I pull my knees to my chest and wrap my arms around them and stare at the door, and I don't move. I don't go out. I don't follow.

I'm very good at not following. I've had practice.

* * *

At 2:15, the deadbolt turns.

The door opens, and cold air rushes in, and Owen steps inside. He's wearing his coat and boots and a headlamp, switched off. His cheeks are red with cold. When he sees me sitting on the couch in the dark, he jumps.

"Jesus, Han. You scared me."

"Where were you?"

"The generator." He pulls off his gloves. "It was making a weird noise. I thought I'd check it before it died on us."

"The generator's off. It turns off at midnight."

"Yeah, I know, I meant." He stops. Starts again. "I heard something. Out by the shed. I wanted to make sure it wasn't a bear getting into the trash."

"Was it?"

"No. Nothing there." He crosses to the stove, holds his hands out to it. His back is to me. "Probably just the wind."

"Did you hear anybody calling?"

His hands go still over the stove.

"No," Owen says, without turning around. "Why? Did you?"

I look at his back. At the snow melting on the shoulders of his coat. At his boots, leaving wet prints on the floor.

"No," I say. "Just the wind."

sections.title: Chapter 6
sections.html:
Chapter 6

Rule #6: Do not hike past the red blazes.

In the morning, Owen wants to hike.

"Fresh air," he says. "Clear our heads. Get out of this cabin for a while." He's already lacing his boots. "There's a trail that goes around the lake. Mara says the views are incredible."

I clip the orange satellite messenger to my backpack. Owen raises an eyebrow but doesn't say anything this time.

The trail starts at the far edge of the meadow and winds down through the pines toward the lake. Every hundred yards or so, there's a small rectangle of paint on a tree trunk, bright blue, marking the way. The air is sharp and clean and smells like cold water and sap. For the first hour, it's almost nice. Owen holds my hand on the steep parts. He points out a woodpecker. He makes a terrible pun about the lake being so shore of itself, and I laugh despite myself.

At the head of the lake, the trail splits.

The blue blazes go left, following the shore. To the right, a narrower path climbs steeply into the trees, up toward the long ridge that leads to the Anvil. On the first tree along that path, there's a blaze painted red.

"Rule six," I say.

"Come on." Owen's already starting up the right-hand path. "Just a little way. Mara said there's an overlook up there. You can see the whole valley."

"Mara said not to go past the red blazes."

"Mara said a lot of things." He turns and looks at me, and there's something in his face I don't recognize. Something hard. "Aren't you curious, Han? Don't you want to see it?"

"See what?"

He doesn't answer. He just holds out his hand.

I should say no. I know I should say no.

I take his hand.

* * *

We climb for forty minutes. The trail gets narrower and rockier. The trees thin out. The wind picks up, cold and relentless, coming straight off the snowfields above. My thighs burn. My lungs burn. Owen doesn't slow down.

And then we come out of the last of the trees onto a bare rock shoulder, and there it is.

The Anvil.

A huge block of gray granite jutting out over nothing, flat on top, like a platform. Beyond it, the cliff drops away so suddenly it makes my stomach lurch. Six hundred feet, straight down, to a jumble of broken rock and scree and a thin silver thread of creek.

And at the base of the Anvil, on the flat rock where the trail ends, there's a cairn.

A small pile of stones, carefully stacked, about three feet high. On the top stone, someone has painted words in white.

DANIEL MERCER. 1988–2023. THE MOUNTAIN KNOWS.

I stop walking.

Owen stops beside me. He's breathing hard. He's looking at the cairn. And then, slowly, he turns and looks at me.

"Who's Daniel Mercer?" he asks.

His voice is perfectly casual. Mildly curious. The way you'd ask about a name on a plaque in a park.

I look at the cairn. At the white letters. The mountain knows.

And I do what I've always done. I let my eyes fill with tears. I let my chin tremble. I put my hand over my mouth, and I make a small, broken sound, and I let my knees go weak so that Owen has to catch me.

"That's him," I whisper. "That was my husband."

I cry in all the right places.

And over my shoulder, holding me, my new husband looks at the cairn for a very long time without saying anything at all.

sections.title: Chapter 7
sections.html:
Chapter 7

Rule #5: The radio is for emergencies only. Channel 9. Mara will answer.

Owen apologizes all the way back down the mountain. He didn't know. He had no idea. He never would have taken me up there if he'd known. He's so sorry, Han. He's so, so sorry.

I say it's okay. I say he couldn't have known. I hold his hand.

That afternoon, while he's out chopping wood, I pick up the radio.

It sits on a shelf by the door: a squat black base unit with a coiled handset and a glowing red dial. It's set to channel nine. There's a strip of masking tape under the dial with one word written on it in marker. MARA.

I don't press the talk button. I just turn up the volume, and listen.

Static. The hiss of empty air.

And then, very faint, a woman's voice. Not talking to me. Talking to someone else.

"—still hasn't cracked. I watched her at the cairn. Not a flicker."

Mara.

A man's voice answers. Crackly, distorted, too faint to recognize.

"—patience. Three more nights. She'll—"

A burst of static swallows the rest.

"—told you she was cold," Mara says. "I told you three years ago. You didn't see her at the funeral. She didn't shed a real tear the whole—"

I stand very still by the radio with my hand over my mouth.

The man's voice again. I lean closer. I can't make out the words.

And then, outside, the sound of the axe stops.

I turn the volume down. I step away from the radio. By the time Owen opens the door, stamping snow off his boots, I'm at the stove, stirring a pot of soup.

"You okay?" he asks. "You look pale."

"Just tired."

He comes up behind me and wraps his arms around my waist and puts his chin on my shoulder, the way he always does.

"Three more nights," Owen says softly. "And then we can go home."

sections.title: Chapter 8
sections.html:
Chapter 8

Rule #8: The root cellar is not part of your stay.

The next morning, Owen drives the Jeep out to the end of the road where there's one bar of cell signal, to call his office. He'll be gone two hours, maybe three. He kisses me goodbye on the porch.

"Lock the door," he says. "Rule two."

"The sun's up."

"Lock it anyway."

I watch the Jeep bump away down the rutted road until the trees swallow it. Then I get the hatchet from the woodbox, and I walk around behind the cabin to the root cellar.

It's a squat wooden door, set into a mound of earth at an angle, like a door into a hill. There's a heavy padlock through the hasp. Brand new. Shiny brass.

The hasp itself is old and rusted, held to the weathered door frame by four screws.

It takes me eleven minutes with the hatchet blade to lever them out. The padlock hangs uselessly from the hasp, still locked. I swing the door open.

Stairs go down into the dark. Six of them, cut into the earth, shored with old timbers. The air that rises up is cold and damp and smells like dirt and potatoes and something else. Something electric. Plastic and warm dust.

The smell of machines.

I turn on my phone's flashlight and go down.

* * *

It's not a root cellar anymore.

There are still a few old wooden shelves along one wall, with a row of dusty Mason jars. But the rest of the small earthen room has been turned into something else.

There's a folding table. On the table, a laptop, closed, plugged into a heavy battery pack. A tangle of cables. A small black box with an antenna. And a plastic crate full of speakers. Weatherproof ones, camouflage-patterned, the kind hunters strap to trees to play animal calls. Six of them. Each with a little antenna.

I open the laptop. It's not password protected. On the screen there's a single program open, a sound board with a grid of buttons. Each button has a label.

HANNAH 1. HANNAH 2. COME OUT. COLD. DARK. FIND ME. SEE YOU ON THE OTHER SIDE.

I press HANNAH 1 with a shaking finger. From the speaker on the table, very soft, Daniel's voice says my name.

I slam the laptop shut.

On the wall above the table, pinned to a sheet of plywood, there's a corkboard.

My face looks back at me from a dozen photographs. Me at Daniel's memorial service, in a black dress, dry-eyed. Me leaving the insurance office in Billings. Me in Denver, getting coffee, jogging, getting into my car. Photos taken from far away, through long lenses. Photos I never knew anyone took.

Newspaper clippings. Widow Collects $1.2 Million. Search Called Off for Missing Billings Hiker. Family of Missing Man Questions Wife's Account.

A copy of the insurance policy.

A copy of my marriage certificate. My second marriage certificate. Hannah Mercer and Owen Pryce, six weeks ago, Denver City and County Building.

And in the center of the board, pinned above everything else, an old photograph, sun-faded, curling at the corners. Two boys on a dock by a lake, maybe ten and twelve, grinning at the camera with their arms around each other's necks, skinny and sunburned and holding up a fish.

The older boy is Daniel. I'd know that grin anywhere.

The younger boy has sandy hair that falls in his eyes, and a crooked smile.

Someone has written on the white border in ballpoint pen: Danny & Luke, Kestrel Lake, 1998.

I stand in the root cellar and look at the photograph for a long time.

Luke. Daniel's little brother. I met him once, at the wedding, for five minutes. He had a beard then, and long hair, and he was drunk, and he left before the cake.

My husband is my dead husband's brother.

Of course he is.

sections.title: Chapter 9
sections.html:
Chapter 9

Rule #7: Keep the woodstove burning. The nights here can kill you.

I put everything back.

I close the laptop and square it on the table. I line up the crate of speakers. I climb the six earthen steps and close the cellar door and fit the old screws back into their holes, and I tighten them with the hatchet blade until the padlock hangs straight and innocent, exactly the way it did before. I brush the wood shavings into the snow with my boot.

Then I go inside and sit at the table and wait for my husband to come home.

While I wait, I'll tell you what really happened on the mountain. You've earned it.

* * *

Daniel Mercer was charming, and funny, and reckless, and he owed four hundred thousand dollars to men in Las Vegas who did not send polite reminder letters.

It started with sports betting on his phone. Then poker. Then a friend of a friend who ran a private game in the back of a steakhouse in Billings, and a line of credit, and a man named Rudy who came to our house one night and sat on our couch and admired our wedding photos and asked, very politely, whether I liked my kneecaps.

Daniel had a life insurance policy. One point two million dollars. His father had made him buy it when we got married.

It was Daniel's idea. I want you to know that. I said no. I said no for a month. And then Rudy's friend broke Daniel's hand in our garage with a car door, and I stopped saying no.

The plan was simple. He knew the Kestrel Valley. He'd grown up hiking it. He'd go up the Anvil trail alone on a gray October day, leave his hat on a bush below the cliff and his water bottle in the creek, then hike out over the back side of the ridge, down a drainage nobody ever used, to a truck he'd left at an old logging road. Drive to Canada. Disappear.

I'd report him missing. I'd cry. I'd collect the insurance. I'd pay Rudy what we owed, through a lawyer, so the debt would die with Daniel. And a year later, I'd wire half of what was left to an account in the Cayman Islands, and Daniel would start over somewhere warm.

I did my part. I cried in all the right places. I paid Rudy. I waited a year.

When I went to wire the money, the account in the Caymans was closed.

I never heard from Daniel again.

For three years, I've believed the mountain really did take him. That somewhere on that back-side drainage, alone, in the snow, he slipped. That the lie we told turned true while nobody was looking. That I'm the only person on earth who knows that Daniel Mercer didn't die on the day everyone thinks he did, and that it doesn't matter, because he's dead anyway.

I've carried that for three years. It's heavy. You have no idea how heavy.

* * *

Owen comes home at two. He brings a bag of groceries from the gas station at the end of the county road: coffee, bread, a box of cheap chocolate donuts because he knows I love them. He kisses me. He tells me about his boss and a client who wants a glass atrium on a house in Aspen.

I smile, and I eat a donut, and I don't tell him I know his name is Luke.

* * *

That night, I keep the woodstove burning. Rule seven. The temperature drops to eight degrees and the logs of the cabin pop and crack in the cold like gunshots.

At 12:52, the voice comes from the trees.

"Hannah."

I'm lying on my back in the dark. Beside me, Owen is lying on his back too. I can tell by his breathing that he's awake.

He's awake, and his hands are on top of the covers where I can feel them. He isn't touching anything. No phone. No remote. I felt him put his phone on the nightstand at eleven and I heard it thunk down, face first, on the wood.

"Hannah. Where's my money?"

Owen goes rigid beside me.

It's the same voice. Daniel's voice. But it's not muffled now. Not tinny. Not playing through a little camouflage speaker strapped to a tree.

It's closer. It's clearer. It's angrier.

And there's no button on that laptop that says WHERE'S MY MONEY.

"You owe me, Han. You owe me half. I'm coming to get it."

Owen sits bolt upright in the bed. In the red glow from the stove, I can see his face. It's gray. His mouth is open. He's staring at the window like he's seen a ghost.

"That's not—" he whispers, and stops.

"Not what?" I ask softly.

He doesn't answer. He just stares at the black window, and his hand finds mine on the blanket, and grips it, hard.

And for the first time since I met him, I think my second husband is as frightened as I am.

sections.title: Chapter 10
sections.html:
Chapter 10

Rule #9: If one of you leaves the cabin at night, the other must not follow.

At dawn, while the coffee brews, I say it.

"Good morning, Luke."

He's standing at the stove with his back to me, feeding in kindling. His hand stops halfway to the firebox. For a long moment he doesn't move at all. Then he puts the stick in, and closes the stove door, and turns around.

He looks exhausted. Older. The crooked smile is gone, and without it his face is Daniel's face, twenty pounds lighter and two years younger. I don't know how I ever missed it.

"How long have you known?" he asks.

"Since yesterday. I found your cellar."

He closes his eyes.

"I'm sorry," he says. "I'm—Hannah, I'm sorry."

"For which part? Spilling coffee on my laptop? Marrying me? Playing my dead husband's voice through the trees so I'd crack and confess to killing him?"

He flinches. "All of it."

"Your mother's in on it."

"It was her idea. Mostly." He sits down heavily at the table. "She never believed you, Han. Never. She said you were too calm at the search. Too calm at the funeral. She said you took the money and didn't even put a headstone on his grave." He rubs his face. "I didn't want to believe her. I really didn't. But then the letters started."

"What letters?"

"Anonymous. To my mom. Typed. Postmarked Missoula. The first one came about a year ago." He looks up at me. "They said you pushed him. They said somebody saw you on the trail that day, when you said you were in Billings. They said if we brought you back to the mountain, you'd break."

"Who sent them?"

"We don't know. Somebody who knew things. Things about Danny, about you, that nobody else knew." He shakes his head. "The letters told us about the rules. The contest. The voice clips. They said, Make her hear him. She'll confess to the mountain."

"And you married me."

"That wasn't in the letters." He says it quietly. "That was me. I just meant to get close to you. Figure out who you were. And then I got close, and I—" He stops. "Some of it wasn't a lie, Hannah."

I look at him. At his hands, wrapped around a coffee mug he hasn't drunk from.

"Last night," I say. "The voice. That wasn't your laptop."

"No." He looks at the window, at the pale light coming over the ridge. "I didn't play anything last night. I didn't play anything the night before, either, the second time. I went outside at midnight to turn the speakers on, the way I did the first night, and I heard him before I even got to the cellar. Out in the trees. Calling you."

"And you didn't follow."

"Rule nine," Luke says, with a broken laugh. "My mom wrote that one for you. So you'd never catch me."

He puts his head in his hands.

"Hannah. What is out there?"

I pour two cups of coffee. I set one in front of him. I sit down across from him, and I wrap my hands around my own mug, and I tell him the truth. Rudy, the debt, the hat on the bush, the drainage on the back side of the ridge, the truck on the logging road, the account in the Caymans that closed.

When I'm done, Luke doesn't say anything for a long time.

"You're lying," he says finally.

"You heard him last night."

"You're—" His voice breaks. "He's my brother. He wouldn't. He wouldn't let our mom think—three years, Hannah. She's been putting flowers on an empty grave for three years."

"I know."

"He'd never—"

"Where's my money, Han?" I say quietly. "You heard him."

Luke looks at me across the table with his dead brother's eyes, and I watch the last three years fall apart in his face.

Then he gets up, and crosses to the radio, and picks up the handset.

"Mom," he says. "You need to come over here. Right now."

sections.title: Chapter 11
sections.html:
Chapter 11

Rule #5: Mara will answer.

Mara comes across the valley in her plow truck in forty minutes flat. She walks into the cabin with her rifle over her shoulder and snow on her boots, and she looks at Luke, and then at me, and her face goes hard as granite.

"She knows," she says.

"She knows," Luke says. "Mom, sit down. You need to hear this."

"I don't need to hear anything from—"

"Mom. Sit down."

She sits. She keeps the rifle across her knees.

I tell it again. All of it. Mara doesn't move while I talk. She doesn't blink. When I get to the part about the truck on the logging road, her knuckles go white on the rifle stock.

When I'm finished, she says, very quietly, "Liar."

"Mom," Luke says. "I heard him. Last night. And the night before. That wasn't the laptop. That wasn't anything we did."

"It's a trick. She's got someone out there. A boyfriend. A—"

"He said, Where's my money."

Mara stops.

"The letters," I say. "The ones from Missoula. What did they say, exactly?"

Mara stares at me. Then, slowly, she reaches into the inside pocket of her canvas coat and takes out a bundle of envelopes tied with a rubber band. She's been carrying them. Of course she has. She tosses them on the table.

I pick up the top one and unfold it. Typed, on plain white paper. No signature.

She told the rangers she was in Billings that day. She wasn't. She was on the Anvil trail. She knew exactly where he'd be standing.

And the next one: Bring her back to the valley. Make it a prize, something she'll want. Give her rules to follow. She was always good at rules. Then make her hear him. Use the old videos. She'll crack.

And the next: She'll be on guard. She has a thing about Daniel's voice. Play it at night, from the trees. Tell her not to go outside. Tell her the voice isn't real. That's what will break her. Being told what she knows isn't true.

I set the letter down.

"Mara," I say. "Who knew I was on the Anvil trail that day?"

She doesn't answer.

"Nobody," I say. "Nobody but me and Daniel. Because I drove him to the trailhead. At six in the morning. And then I drove back to Billings and made sure the whole town saw me at the grocery store at ten. Nobody could have written that letter. Nobody but Daniel."

The cabin is so quiet I can hear the snow ticking against the windows.

Mara Voss looks down at the letters in front of her. Her hands are shaking. The rifle slides off her knees and clatters to the floor, and she doesn't pick it up.

"He wrote them," she whispers. "He's alive. He's been alive this whole time, and he let me—"

She can't finish.

Luke crouches beside her chair and puts his arms around her, and his big, rawboned mother presses her face into his shoulder and makes a sound I'll never forget. Not crying. Something older and deeper than crying. The sound of a woman who has grieved for three years discovering that she was only a tool.

I look out the window.

It's started to snow.

sections.title: Chapter 12
sections.html:
Chapter 12

Rule #7: The nights here can kill you.

By noon, it's a whiteout.

The snow comes down so thick and fast that I can't see the edge of the meadow from the porch. The wind drives it sideways. The temperature is plunging. Luke goes out to check the vehicles and comes back ten minutes later white-faced, with snow caked on his eyebrows.

"All four tires on the Jeep," he says. "Slashed. Mom's truck, too. And the distributor cap's gone."

Mara stands up so fast her chair scrapes. "He's here. He's been here the whole time."

"The radio," I say.

Luke is already at the shelf by the door. He picks up the handset. Presses the button. "Kestrel base, this is Stillwater, come in." Nothing. Not even static. He turns the unit around. On the back, where the antenna cable should screw in, there's nothing. Someone has cut it clean through, right at the wall.

"When?" Mara says. "When did he get in here?"

"The first night," Luke says slowly. "When I went out to turn on the speakers. I left the door unlocked."

I go to my backpack in the bedroom. I don't hurry. I don't want them to see me hurry. I unzip the front pocket where I clip the orange satellite messenger every night.

It's gone.

I stand there with my hand in the empty pocket.

"Hannah?" Luke's in the doorway. "What is it?"

"My satellite messenger," I say. "It's gone too."

He closes his eyes. "So we can't call anyone."

"No."

"No phone signal for fifty miles. No radio. No vehicles. And a blizzard." Luke laughs, a terrible, cracked little sound. "And my dead brother out there somewhere in the trees."

I zip the backpack closed.

"Rule seven," I say. "Keep the woodstove burning."

sections.title: Chapter 13
sections.html:
Chapter 13

Rule #2: Lock the door at dusk.

Dusk comes early in a blizzard. By four-thirty, it's nearly dark. We lock the door. We bolt the shutters on the windows. Luke fills every pot and pan with water from the pump, in case. Mara loads her rifle and sits in the rocking chair facing the door, and doesn't move.

We don't turn on the lights. The generator runs from six until midnight, but none of us can stand the idea of being lit up from the inside, a lantern in the dark for anyone to see. We sit in the red glow of the woodstove and wait.

At 9:14, someone knocks on the door.

Three knocks. Slow. Unhurried.

Mara raises the rifle.

"Mom," says a voice on the other side of the door. "Mom, it's me."

Mara makes a small sound. The rifle barrel dips.

"It's freezing out here, Mom. Aren't you going to let me in?"

"Danny?" Mara's voice is barely a whisper.

"Hey, Mom." A soft laugh through the wood. That laugh. I'd know it anywhere. "Long time. I know. I'm sorry. I'm really, really sorry. I can explain everything, I swear. Just open the door."

Mara is on her feet. She takes a step toward the door.

"Mom, don't," Luke says. "Rule two."

"He's my son."

"He let you bury an empty box." Luke steps between her and the door. "He wrote you those letters. He's been out there all week, calling Hannah's name, cutting the throat of a fox on our porch. Mom. Look at me. That's not Danny. Not our Danny. Not anymore."

On the other side of the door, silence.

Then Daniel laughs again. It's different this time. Flat.

"Hey, little brother," he says. "Nice work, by the way. I didn't think you'd actually marry her. That was above and beyond."

Luke's jaw tightens. "Why, Danny?"

"Why what?"

"Why any of it? Why make us think she killed you? Why not just come home?"

"Because I can't come home, Luke. I'm dead. Dead men don't get to have bank accounts." The voice moves, like he's leaning against the door. "And my loving wife has one point two million dollars that belongs to me, and she wouldn't give it back."

"You closed the account," I say.

Silence on the other side.

"I tried to send it," I say. "A year later. Like we planned. The account was closed. I didn't have any way to reach you."

"Hannah." Daniel says my name like he's tasting it. "Hi, Han. You sound good. Married life agrees with you."

"What do you want, Daniel?"

"What I've always wanted." His voice is pleasant. Almost warm. "What's mine. There's a satellite phone in my pocket with a data connection and a nice new bank account waiting on the other end. You're going to open the door, and come outside, and log into your bank, and send me every penny that's left. And then I'll go away, and you'll never hear from me again."

"And if I don't?"

He's quiet for a moment.

"There are twenty gallons of gas in the shed," Daniel says. "For the generator. And these old log cabins, Han. They go up like matchsticks."

sections.title: Chapter 14
sections.html:
Chapter 14

Rule #9: The other must not follow.

"He's bluffing," Mara says. "He wouldn't. His own mother is in here."

It's past ten. Daniel has been quiet for an hour. We haven't heard him leave. We haven't heard anything but the wind.

"The fox, Mom," Luke says quietly. "He cut its throat and left it on the porch. For fun. For theater." He's sitting on the floor with his back against the wall, the rifle across his lap now. Mara gave it to him an hour ago, without a word. "Three years ago I'd have said Danny would never hurt anything. I don't know who that is out there."

"How much is left?" Mara asks me. "The money."

I look at the stove. "About seven hundred thousand."

"Then give it to him."

"Mom—"

"Give it to him, Hannah." Mara's voice is raw. "Give him the money and let him go. I don't care about the money. I don't care about any of it. I just want everybody to walk out of this valley alive."

I want to say yes. I want it more than anything.

But I was married to Daniel for six years. And I know something his mother doesn't.

"The second I send that money," I say, "I'm the only person alive who knows he faked his death. Me and the two of you. Three witnesses. And he'll be standing right there, on the porch, with twenty gallons of gasoline."

Nobody says anything.

Outside, very close, Daniel starts to sing.

It's a campfire song. Something silly. Something the Mercer boys must have sung as kids, on this lake, in the summers, because I watch Luke's face crumple, and I watch Mara put her hand over her mouth.

Luke gets to his feet.

"No," Mara says. "Luke. No."

"He's my brother." He checks the rifle. "Maybe I can still talk to him. He always listened to me, when we were kids. I was the only one who could talk him down."

"Rule nine," I say. "If one of you leaves the cabin at night—"

"The other must not follow." Luke looks at me for a long moment. Something moves in his face. "You never did follow, did you, Han? Not once. Not even the first night."

"No."

"That's what my mom said. That's how she knew you'd done something." A strange, sad smile. "People who have nothing to hide go outside. They run toward the voice."

He unlocks the door, and steps out into the dark and the snow, and pulls it closed behind him.

Mara lunges for the door. I grab her arm.

"Let go of me!"

"Rule nine," I say. "If you go out there, he has both of you."

She stares at me with wild eyes. And then something in her gives, and she sags against the door, and I lock it, and slide the bolt home.

Outside, the singing stops.

sections.title: Chapter 15
sections.html:
Chapter 15

Rule #3: Your spouse is in bed with you.

We hear them for a while.

Voices, out in the snow. Low, then louder. Luke's voice, pleading. Daniel's voice, laughing. We can't make out the words. Mara stands with her ear pressed to the door and her eyes squeezed shut, and I stand beside her and hold her hand, and I don't know when that happened, but neither of us lets go.

Then Luke shouts something. Sharp. Angry.

Then a gunshot.

It cracks across the valley and comes back off the mountains, again and again, a rolling echo that goes on forever.

Then nothing.

Mara makes a sound like an animal. I hold on to her with both arms.

A long time passes. Five minutes, maybe. Maybe an hour. The stove ticks. The wind moans.

Then footsteps on the porch. Slow. Heavy. Crunching through the snow.

Three knocks.

"Hannah," says Daniel's voice, through the door. "Luke tripped. It's a real shame. He's hurt pretty bad." A pause. "He's out by the woodshed. He's going to freeze to death in about an hour, I'd guess, if somebody doesn't bring him inside."

Mara is shaking so hard I can feel it in my own bones.

"So here's the new deal," Daniel says pleasantly. "You open the door. You come out. We take a little walk, you and me, and you do some online banking. And then Mom can go get her other son."

"Hannah," Mara whispers. "Please."

I look at the door. At the iron bolt.

I think about the letter. She was always good at rules.

"Okay," I say, loud enough for him to hear. "Okay, Daniel. I'm coming out."

I sit down on the floor, and I unlace my left hiking boot, and I pull it off. Mara stares at me like I've lost my mind.

I pull up the insole. Underneath it, in a hollow I cut into the foam with a kitchen knife in Denver three weeks ago, there's a second orange satellite messenger. Smaller than the first one. Newer.

I press my thumb on the SOS button and hold it down until the little light blinks green.

Then I put my boot back on, and I lace it tight.

"What is that?" Mara whispers. "Where did you—"

"Keep the stove burning," I tell her. "Help is coming. When you hear them, go get Luke."

And I unlock the door.

sections.title: Chapter 16
sections.html:
Chapter 16

Rule #4: Do not feed anything that comes to the porch.

The cold hits me like a wall of broken glass.

The snow is still falling, but softer now, big lazy flakes drifting down through the beam of a headlamp. The headlamp is on Daniel's forehead. Behind it, I can't see his face, just a dark shape in a long coat, and the glint of a pistol in his gloved hand.

"Hi, Han," he says.

"Hi, Daniel."

He tilts his head, and the headlamp beam slides off my face and down, and in the spill of light I finally see him.

He's thinner. So much thinner. His cheeks are hollow under a matted beard, and there's a raw red patch on the side of his nose where frostbite has taken the skin. His eyes are the same gray as Mara's, as Luke's. But there's something missing in them now. Something that used to be warm.

"You look good," he says. "Really good. Denver suits you."

"You've been watching me."

"For a while." He gestures with the pistol. "Walk. Woodshed. Let's go see my brother."

* * *

Luke is lying on his side in the snow at the open door of the woodshed, curled around his left leg. There's blood on the snow, black in the headlamp light. A lot of it. His face is gray, and his teeth are chattering so hard I can hear them.

I drop to my knees beside him before Daniel can stop me.

"Luke. Luke, look at me."

His eyes find mine. "Han," he whispers. "Told you. Rule nine."

The bullet went through his thigh, above the knee. It missed the artery; if it hadn't, he'd already be dead. But he's lost a lot of blood, and he's lying in the snow, and his lips are going blue. I yank off my scarf and knot it around his leg above the wound and pull it tight, and he screams through his teeth.

"Touching," Daniel says behind me.

"He's your brother."

"He came out here with a rifle to shoot me, Han." Daniel sounds almost amused. "He had it coming." He crouches beside me and holds out a chunky black satellite phone, the kind with a stubby antenna. "Here's how this goes. You log in to your bank. You send it all to the account number I give you. The second I see it land, you can drag Lukey back to Mom, and I'll walk away into the trees, and you'll never see me again."

"The bank sends a code to my phone. There's no cell signal."

"I know. That's why I called them from Missoula last month, pretending to be you, and asked them to send your codes by email instead." He smiles. "You really should use better security questions, Han. Your first pet's name? Come on."

I take the satellite phone.

sections.title: Chapter 17
sections.html:
Chapter 17

Rule #6: Do not hike past the red blazes.

It takes a long time. The satellite connection is slow, and the bank's website doesn't want to load, and my fingers are so cold I keep mistyping. Daniel crouches beside me with the pistol resting on his knee, watching the screen over my shoulder. Beside us, in the snow, Luke drifts in and out.

"Why didn't you come back for it?" I ask while the page spins. "The money. You could have just called me. I'd have sent it."

"You didn't, though."

"The account was closed, Daniel."

"I closed it." He says it matter-of-factly. "About two weeks after I disappeared. I couldn't have a trail leading from you to me, Han. I needed to know you'd wait for me. I needed to know you'd hold on to it." His voice changes. "And then I came down to Billings, a year later, to get you. And you'd sold the house."

"I moved to Denver."

"You moved to Denver. You changed your number. You started over like I'd never existed." The headlamp beam doesn't waver. "I spent two winters in a trapper's shack up in that drainage, living on canned beans and snowmelt, waiting for my wife. And my wife went on dates."

"You let everyone think you were dead."

"I was dead. That was the whole point." He jabs a finger at the screen. "Log in."

I log in. The balance comes up. $712,406.19.

Daniel lets out a long breath. "There she is."

He reads me an account number from memory. I type it in. I type in the amount. My finger hovers over the button that says CONFIRM TRANSFER.

"What happens after?" I ask.

"I told you. I walk away."

"And the three people who know you're alive?"

He's quiet for a moment. The snow falls between us.

"You know what's funny?" Daniel says. "The whole valley already thinks you're crazy. The widow who came back to the mountain where her husband died. Hearing his voice at night. Mom's been telling the lady at the Dunmore post office about it all week, how worried she is about her son's new wife. How unstable she seems." He smiles. "Tragic, when a grieving woman sets fire to a cabin with her new family inside, and then walks up to the Anvil at dawn and steps off. The mountain takes another one."

"Your mother is in that cabin."

"My mother buried an empty box and moved on with her life." His voice goes flat. "Everyone moved on. Everyone except me."

I look at the screen. At the button.

I press it.

Your transfer is being processed. Large transfers may be held for review for up to 24 hours.

Daniel stares at the screen.

"Held," he says.

"It's seven hundred thousand dollars, Daniel. They're going to call me to confirm. That's how banks work."

For a long moment, he doesn't move. Then he stands up, and takes the phone out of my hands, and looks down at me with his dead gray eyes in the glare of his headlamp.

"Then I guess we wait twenty-four hours," he says. "Get up. We're going to the shed. I need to get the gas."

sections.title: Chapter 18
sections.html:
Chapter 18

Rule #7: Keep the woodstove burning.

The generator shed is a small wooden building behind the cabin, humming faintly. The generator itself is off, silent, but the shed still smells like exhaust and gasoline. Along one wall, there are four red plastic cans.

Daniel makes me carry two of them. He carries the other two in one hand, easily, and keeps the pistol in the other.

"You don't have to do this," I say as we slog back through the snow toward the cabin. "The money's coming. You'll have it tomorrow. You can be in Canada by—"

"By the time they find three bodies in a burned cabin?" He shakes his head. "No, Han. The money's not enough anymore. I need to be dead again. Really dead. And the only way to be sure is if there's nobody left who knows otherwise."

"Luke's still alive."

"Not for long."

We come around the corner of the cabin. The porch is dark. The windows are shuttered. A thin line of red glow shows under the door. Keep the woodstove burning. Mara's inside, with Luke's rifle, if she had the sense to bring it in. I don't know. I don't know anything.

"Put them down," Daniel says. "Open them."

I set the cans on the porch. I unscrew the caps. The smell of gasoline rises up, thick and sweet, burning the inside of my nose.

"Now splash them. The walls. The door. Go on."

I pick up one can. I turn to the wall of the cabin. My hands are shaking.

And then I turn around and throw the gasoline in his face.

* * *

He screams.

It's a high, animal sound. The gas hits him full in the eyes and the mouth and he staggers back, clawing at his face, and the pistol goes off, a wild shot into the sky. I swing the empty can at his head with everything I have. It bounces off his shoulder. He grabs for me blindly and catches my coat and we go down together in the snow at the bottom of the porch steps.

He's heavier than me. He's stronger. He gets on top of me and his hand is on my throat, squeezing, and his face is right above mine, streaming with gas and tears, his eyes red and swollen shut.

"You owe me," he snarls. "You owe me, Han—"

There's a sound like an axe hitting wood.

Daniel's grip loosens. He tips sideways, slowly, and falls into the snow beside me.

Luke is standing over us. He's on one leg, swaying, holding a log from the woodpile in both hands like a baseball bat. His face is gray as ash. His lips are blue. The scarf around his thigh is soaked through.

"Told you," Luke says, through chattering teeth. "Only one who could talk him down."

Then his leg gives out, and he collapses beside his brother in the snow.

The cabin door bangs open. Mara stands in the light with the rifle, staring down at her two sons lying side by side in the snow.

And Daniel moves.

He's on his hands and knees. He's up. He's running, half blind, staggering, away from the cabin, across the meadow, into the dark and the trees.

Toward the lake. Toward the trail.

Toward the Anvil.

sections.title: Chapter 19
sections.html:
Chapter 19

Rule #9: If one of you leaves the cabin at night, the other must not follow.

We drag Luke inside, Mara and I, one of us under each arm. We lay him on the rug in front of the stove. I retie the tourniquet. I pack the wound with dish towels. Mara piles every blanket in the cabin on top of him and kneels by his head, stroking his hair, whispering to him like he's six years old.

"Is anyone coming?" she asks me. "That thing in your boot. Is it real?"

"It's real."

"Then where are they?"

"It's a blizzard, Mara. They can't fly a helicopter in this. They'll come by snowmobile. It'll take time."

She looks at Luke's face. It's so pale.

"Time," she says. "Time."

I look at the door.

Out there somewhere, in the dark, in the snow, Daniel is climbing toward the Anvil. Half blind. Soaked in gasoline. In eight degrees.

The nights here can kill you.

I think about the rules. I think about how good I've always been at following them. How I stayed in the car at the trailhead three years ago and watched him walk away into the trees. How I sat on the couch and didn't open the door. How I stayed in the bed. How I never, ever followed.

People who have nothing to hide go outside. They run toward the voice.

I stand up. I put on my coat. I take the headlamp from the hook by the door.

"Where are you going?" Mara says.

"To find your son."

"Hannah." Her voice cracks. "Rule nine."

"I know," I say. "I'm breaking it."

sections.title: Chapter 20
sections.html:
Chapter 20

Rule #6: Do not hike past the red blazes.

The snow has almost stopped. The sky is starting to go gray in the east. I follow his tracks in the beam of the headlamp: deep, staggering holes in the fresh snow, weaving across the meadow, down through the pines, along the lakeshore. Past the fork. Past the first red blaze.

Up.

It's so much harder in the snow. I fall, and get up, and fall again. My lungs are on fire. My legs are shaking. The cold is a living thing, clawing at my face, trying to get into my coat. The blazes go by in the gray light, one by one, splashes of red on the black trees, like drops of blood.

I come out of the trees onto the bare rock shoulder just as the sun comes over the ridge.

The whole valley turns gold. The lake below, the snowy meadows, the black pines, all of it glowing, so beautiful it takes the last of my breath away.

And there, at the end of the Anvil, standing at the very edge of the cliff with his back to me, is Daniel.

* * *

"Don't," I say.

He doesn't turn around. He's standing on the flat granite, right at the lip, where the rock just stops and the air begins. Six hundred feet of nothing below him. His coat is frozen stiff with gasoline. His hands are bare and white.

"Funny," he says. His voice is hoarse, cracking. "This is where it all started. I stood right here three years ago. Threw my hat over. Watched it catch on that bush down there. I remember thinking, This is it. This is the day I get to start over."

"You still can."

"Can I?" He laughs. It turns into a cough. "They're coming, aren't they? You called them. Somehow."

"Yes."

"You always did have a plan, Han." He sways a little on the edge. My heart stops. "You know what I figured out, those two winters in the shack? You never loved me. Not really. You loved the idea of being rescued. And when I couldn't rescue you anymore, you rescued yourself. With my money. With my death."

"That's not true."

"It's a little true."

Below us, faint across the valley, I hear engines. The high whine of snowmobiles. Headlights, three of them, moving along the lakeshore trail. Coming this way.

Daniel hears them too.

He turns around, finally, and looks at me. His eyes are swollen almost shut. His face is raw and red.

"See you on the other side, Han," he says. The last thing he said to me in the parking lot at the trailhead, three years ago.

And he steps back off the edge.

* * *

I've never followed.

Not once. Not ever. I'm very good at staying still. At waiting. At watching from a safe distance. It's the thing I'm best at in the world.

But my body moves before my mind does.

I'm across the rock. I'm diving. I'm flat on my stomach on the frozen granite with my arms over the edge, and my hands are locked around his wrist, and his whole weight is hanging from me, pulling me forward, my shoulders screaming, the rock scraping my chest, sliding, sliding.

He looks up at me. Hanging over six hundred feet of air. Astonished.

"Han," he says. "What are you doing?"

"I don't know," I sob. "I don't know. Hold on."

"Let go."

"No."

We hang there. I don't know how long. Long enough that I stop feeling my hands. Long enough that I think I'm going to go over with him.

Then there are boots on the rock behind me. And hands on my coat. And hands reaching past me, over the edge, grabbing Daniel's arm, his collar, his coat. Voices shouting. Pull! Pull!

And Daniel Mercer comes up over the edge of the Anvil, and lands on the rock beside me, gasping, alive.

Three years late.

sections.title: Chapter 21
sections.html:
Chapter 21

Rule #1: When the lights go out, stay in bed.

Luke keeps his leg.

It's close. He loses a lot of blood, and the helicopter can't get in until noon, when the clouds finally lift. But Mara keeps the woodstove burning, and keeps him warm, and keeps talking to him, and when the flight nurses finally carry him out of the cabin on a stretcher, he's awake enough to squeeze my hand and whisper, "Rule nine, Han. You broke it."

"I did."

"Good," he says, and passes out.

* * *

Daniel Mercer is charged with attempted murder, kidnapping, extortion, arson, insurance fraud, and a list of federal crimes so long his public defender reportedly laughed when she read it. He pleads guilty to most of them. He'll be in prison until he's an old man.

He doesn't look at his mother at the sentencing. Mara sits in the front row anyway, straight-backed, with Luke on crutches beside her. She doesn't cry. She just watches him, the whole time, with her son's gray eyes.

I'm charged too. Conspiracy to commit insurance fraud. It's what I deserve.

But I cooperate. I give the federal prosecutors everything: the plan, the dates, the truck on the logging road, the account in the Caymans, Rudy and his friends in Las Vegas. I pay back every cent I have left. I sell my condo. I plead guilty. The judge gives me three years of probation and a thousand hours of community service, and a long, disappointed look over the top of her glasses.

It could have been so much worse. Everyone keeps telling me that. My lawyer. The prosecutor. The judge.

It could have been so much worse.

* * *

Luke and I have the marriage annulled in March. It's quiet and civil. We sign papers in a lawyer's office in Bozeman. Afterward, we get coffee at a place across the street, and neither of us knows what to say.

"For what it's worth," he says finally, stirring his coffee, "I meant it. What I said in the cabin. Some of it wasn't a lie."

"I know."

"The pancakes. The puns. The—" He stops. "All of that was real. The only thing I lied about was my name."

"That's a pretty big thing to lie about."

"Yeah." He smiles his crooked smile. "Yeah, it is."

He spills his coffee when he stands up to leave. All over the table. All over my sleeve.

We both laugh until we cry.

sections.title: Epilogue
sections.html:
Epilogue

Rule #3: Your spouse is in bed with you.

I live in a small apartment in Missoula now. I work at a bakery. I get up at four every morning, in the dark, and make bread, and I'm home by one. It's quiet. It's good. On Sundays, I call Mara. She doesn't always pick up. But sometimes she does.

I've told you a lot of things in this story. Most of them were true.

Not all.

* * *

I told you I never heard from Daniel again after the account closed. That wasn't true.

He called me a year and a half ago. From a pay phone in Missoula, of all places. I was in Denver, in my new apartment, with my new life, and my phone rang at two in the morning, and a voice I'd buried said, Hey, Han. Did you miss me?

He told me he'd been watching me. He told me he wanted his money, all of it, plus interest. He told me that if I went to the police, he'd tell them I'd pushed him off the Anvil and he'd barely survived, and who do you think they'd believe? The grieving husband who crawled out of the wilderness, or the widow who took the money and ran?

Then he hung up. And I understood that he was going to come for me. Not now. When he was ready. When I least expected it.

So I got ready first.

* * *

I told you I didn't recognize Owen Pryce.

I told you I met him in a coffee shop in Denver, when he spilled his cold brew on my laptop. That was true. What I didn't tell you is that I knew exactly who he was before the coffee hit the keyboard.

He'd shaved his beard and cut his hair since the wedding. But I'd spent six years looking at Daniel's face, and Luke had it, underneath. The same jaw. The same gray eyes. The same way of spilling things when he was nervous.

I knew within ten seconds that my dead husband's little brother had come to find me. And I knew he wasn't smart enough to have planned it himself.

Somebody had sent him. Somebody who wanted me back in Montana.

So I let him spill coffee on my laptop. I let him dry it with a hair dryer. I let him make me pancakes at midnight and tell me terrible puns. And when he asked me to marry him, I said yes before he finished the question.

* * *

I told you I bought one satellite messenger.

I bought two. And before I ever set foot in Kestrel Valley, I spent four months, and most of what was left of Daniel's money, on a very good lawyer in Denver. He spent those four months having very quiet conversations with an assistant United States attorney in Billings, and a sheriff in Dunmore, Montana.

The deal was simple. I'd confess to insurance fraud, and pay back what I could. And in exchange for leniency, I'd deliver them the man who'd planned it. A man who'd been legally dead for three years. A man nobody could find.

Nobody but me.

All I had to do was go back to the mountain and let him come to me.

The second messenger in my boot wasn't set to call 911. It was set to call the Dunmore County sheriff's office, where three deputies had been sleeping in their snowmobile suits for a week, waiting for a little green light.

* * *

Everybody thought I walked into their trap.

Mara, with her rules. Luke, with his speakers in the trees. Daniel, with his letters and his fox and his twenty gallons of gasoline.

Everybody thought I was the one being hunted.

I've always been good at following rules. It's the thing I'm best at in the world. But nobody ever asks the obvious question.

Who do you think taught Daniel how to write them?

* * *

Some nights, in my apartment in Missoula, I wake up at 12:52 in the morning, and I lie in the dark, and I listen.

The wind moves in the pines outside my window. The heater ticks. Somewhere across town, a train whistle blows, long and lonely.

And sometimes, very faintly, I think I hear someone call my name.

I don't get up. I don't go to the window. I don't go outside.

I roll over, and I close my eyes, and I go back to sleep.

There's no one in bed beside me. And that's exactly the way I like it.

sections.title: Author’s Note
sections.html:
Author’s Note

Thank you for reading The Cabin Rules.

Every book in this series begins with a list of rules and a woman who breaks them. Nora broke them out of curiosity. Wren broke them out of guilt. With Hannah, I wanted to try something different: a heroine who is better at the rules than the people who wrote them.

I also wanted to write about marriage, and about how well we can ever really know the person lying beside us in the dark. Hannah has two husbands in this book, and neither of them is quite who she thinks. Then again, she isn’t quite who they think, either.

Kestrel Valley, the Anvil, and the town of Dunmore are invented, but anyone who has spent an October night in the Montana backcountry knows how total the dark can be, and how the wind in the pines can sound almost like a voice.

If this story kept you awake past midnight, I’d be grateful if you left a review on Amazon. Reviews are how independent books find their readers, and I read every one.

And if you ever hear someone calling your name from the trees, remember rule three.

— Sunday Pastores
